sentences.text: Massospondylus was a mid-sized member of the sauropodomorph family.
A large neotype specimen is estimated to have reached approximately 5 meters in length.
Another researcher, Gregory S. Paul, estimated the animal's length at 4.3 meters in a 2024 publication.
Frank Seebacher calculated a body weight of 136.7 kilograms based on a 4-meter length assumption.
Richard Owen first described the genus in 1854 using fossils discovered in South Africa.
The original collection held at the Hunterian Museum in London was destroyed by a bomb between May 10 and 11, 1941.
Modern science considers Massospondylus to have been bipedal, correcting earlier views that it walked on four legs.
It was likely a herbivore, although some scientists suggest early sauropodomorphs might have eaten both plants and meat.
The animal possessed a sharp claw on each thumb, possibly used to uproot plants or pull down branches.
Fossilized clutches containing embryos represent some of the oldest known amniote eggs.
The genus includes the type species M. carinatus and the species M. kaalae.
In 1920, von Huene established the group Prosauropoda to unite early long-necked dinosaurs like Massospondylus.
Later, in 1932, von Huene named Sauropodomorpha, which included his Prosauropoda and Sauropoda, moving Massospondylus out of Theropoda.
Massospondylus lived during the Hettangian, Sinemurian, and Pliensbachian ages of the Early Jurassic.
This corresponds to the early Jurassic period, spanning from 200 to 183 million years ago in Africa.
Most fossils come from the upper Elliot and Clarens formations in South Africa and Lesotho.
Remains have also been found in the Forest Sandstone and Mpandi Formation of Zimbabwe.
Additional fossils exist in the Lower Maleri and Takli formations of India, the Kayenta Formation of the US, and the Cañón del Colorado Formation of Argentina.
It is debated whether Owen's assignment of bones to Massospondylus, Pachyspondylus, or Leptospondylus was arbitrary, a view supported by Hans-Dieter Sues in 2004.
Researchers Paul Barrett and Kimberley Chapelle speculated that early neglect of the species was due to Owen's perfunctory descriptions lacking illustrations.
Scientists question whether all previously identified specimens from southern Africa belong to this genus due to the discovery of new genera.
In 1906, von Huene believed that M. hislopi and M. rawesi were not dinosaurs.
A 2004 review classified M. hislopi as an indeterminate sauropodomorph and M. rawesi as an indeterminate theropod.
